# contextbill

> Local-first cost analysis for coding agents. Reads the transcripts already on your
> disk and prices them at published first-party API rates: which sessions ran expensive,
> which produced nothing, and how much of the total is fixed context loaded on every
> turn. The command line reads Claude Code transcripts and, on request, OpenAI
> Codex CLI rollouts; the hosted app reads Claude Code transcripts only.

contextbill exists because per-seat billing reports one number a month, which is
enough to know you spent money and not enough to know where. It ships in two
forms that share one analysis engine, so both produce the same figures for the
same input.

## What it does

- Prices every turn against a dated rate table, split by model, and by whether
  tokens were input, output, a cache write or a cache read. The table carries
  first-party rates from two vendors, each with its own reading date: Anthropic
  (read 2026-09-03) and OpenAI (read 2026-09-07).
- Separates the startup prefix (system prompt, tool catalog, connector
  definitions, instruction files) from the work you actually asked for. That
  prefix is written to cache once and re-read on every subsequent turn, so a
  long session pays for it repeatedly. On the corpus it was built against —
  2,424 transcripts, measured 2026-09-09 — it was 19.6% of the bill.
- Attributes spend to categories such as browser automation, shell, file
  operations and connector catalogs, so the expensive habit is identifiable.
- Corrects two ways the same request gets counted twice, and states the size of
  each correction rather than asserting it. Claude Code rewrites a streamed
  message into the transcript several times and each line restates that
  message's cumulative usage, so summing lines multiplied the total by 2.39x on
  that corpus. A resumed session then copies its parent's history into a new
  file, which double-counted a further $1,250.33 of $15,733.14 until those
  copies were merged across transcripts.
- Reports subscription rate-limit windows, on the command line only, with
  `--limits`. Those come from the API response headers by way of Claude Code, so
  they are the vendor's own count rather than a local estimate; everything
  derived from them is labelled as projected. contextbill never infers a window
  from local files, and says it cannot see one rather than guessing.
- Keeps saved reports so a number can be compared against itself over time.

## What it reads

Command line:

- `~/.claude/projects` by default: Claude Code transcripts, opened read-only.
- `~/.codex/sessions` **only when asked** with `--source codex` or `--source all`:
  OpenAI Codex CLI rollouts. A default run never opens that tree or any path
  outside the Claude Code root.

Hosted web app:

- Claude Code transcripts only, from a directory the user picks, parsed in the
  browser tab. It has no Codex reader.

Both, from every file: token counts, model ids, timestamps, tool names and the
byte size of tool results. Never prompts or completions.

## The two surfaces

- **Command line**: `npx contextbill`. Zero runtime dependencies, no network
  access of any kind, writes a self-contained HTML report. Nothing is uploaded.
- **Hosted web app**: https://contextbill.vercel.app. Transcripts are parsed in
  the browser tab. Only aggregates reach the server: totals, per-model spend,
  per-category spend and per-session counts. Message content is never
  transmitted, and the database has no column that could store it.

## Privacy

- https://contextbill.vercel.app/privacy. What is stored, what is not, and why
  there is no cookie consent banner (the only cookie is the auth session).
- Project folder names encode an operating system username, so they are redacted
  before any report is saved.
- Row-level security in Postgres restricts every row to the account that created
  it.

## Accuracy note

Every figure is an estimate, not an invoice. Three limits, largest first.

Figures are API-equivalent: every dollar is what that usage would cost metered
at the vendor's published first-party API rates, Anthropic's for Claude Code and
OpenAI's for Codex. Most Claude Code usage is on a subscription, which bills a
flat fee, so the totals value the usage rather than restate what anyone was
charged. Bedrock, Vertex and Azure OpenAI are partner-operated, priced separately
again, and are not modelled.

A model with no entry in the rate table is counted, named, and kept out of every
dollar figure rather than folded in at zero. Two are deliberately unpriced today
because the table cannot yet express a per-model cache multiplier, so a total
covering them is understated and says so.

A transcript records how many tokens were written to cache but not which cache
lifetime was billed, so contextbill assumes the cheaper one and tends to
understate rather than overstate.

The startup-prefix figure is a model of how fixed overhead is apportioned, not a
line item any provider bills separately.
